100.statement: A RISC processor must have more complex instructions than a CISC processor.
100.explanation: RISC generally uses a smaller or simpler instruction set.
100.correction: RISC generally uses a smaller or simpler instruction set.

101.statement: GPUs are well suited to carrying out many similar calculations in parallel.
101.explanation: Their many processing units are designed for high-throughput work.

102.statement: A multicore CPU can execute only one independent task at a time.
102.explanation: Different cores can run independent threads at the same time.
102.correction: Different cores can run independent threads at the same time.

103.statement: The best processor architecture depends on the tasks and their characteristics.
103.explanation: Workload, power and cost may favour different designs.

104.statement: A microphone is an output device because it produces sound.
104.explanation: A microphone captures sound and acts as an input device.
104.correction: A microphone captures sound and acts as an input device.

105.statement: Flash storage keeps data without power and has no spinning disk.

106.statement: ROM usually loses its saved contents whenever power is switched off.
106.explanation: ROM is non-volatile; ordinary RAM is volatile.
106.correction: ROM is non-volatile; ordinary RAM is volatile.

107.statement: An operating system manages resources such as memory and running processes.
107.explanation: Resource management is one of its central functions.

108.statement: Paging requires every process to occupy one contiguous block of physical memory.
108.explanation: Pages can map to different physical frames.
108.correction: Pages can map to different physical frames.

109.statement: An interrupt can cause the CPU to execute an interrupt service routine.
109.explanation: The processor responds to the event, then resumes appropriate work.

110.statement: Shortest Job First always selects the process that arrived first.
110.explanation: SJF chooses the shortest eligible job according to its scheduling rules.
110.correction: SJF chooses the shortest eligible job according to its scheduling rules.

111.statement: Round Robin allocates a time slice before moving to another ready process.
111.explanation: A process that has not finished may return to the ready queue.

112.statement: A device driver is the same as a word-processing application.
112.explanation: A driver enables the operating system to communicate with hardware.
112.correction: A driver enables the operating system to communicate with hardware.

113.statement: A disk-cleanup utility performs system maintenance rather than writing a document.
113.explanation: Utility software supports managing or maintaining the system.

114.statement: Open-source software always forbids examination or modification of its source code.
114.explanation: Open-source licences make source available with specified rights.
114.correction: Open-source licences make source available with specified rights.

115.statement: A compiler translates source code into another form before the resulting program is run.
115.explanation: Compilation produces translated output for later execution.

116.statement: Lexical analysis checks full program grammar instead of producing tokens.
116.explanation: Lexical analysis groups characters into tokens; syntax analysis checks structure.
116.correction: Lexical analysis groups characters into tokens; syntax analysis checks structure.

117.statement: A linker combines required modules and references to produce an executable program.
117.explanation: It resolves external references among compiled components.

118.statement: The Waterfall model is based on continuous short iterations with frequent reprioritisation.
118.explanation: Waterfall uses more sequential stages; Agile methods emphasise iteration.
118.correction: Waterfall uses more sequential stages; Agile methods emphasise iteration.

119.statement: Extreme Programming often uses practices such as pair programming and frequent testing.
119.explanation: These practices support rapid feedback and code quality.

120.statement: The Spiral model ignores project risks when selecting its next cycle.
120.explanation: Risk analysis is a defining feature of the Spiral model.
120.correction: Risk analysis is a defining feature of the Spiral model.

121.statement: A trace table should record variable changes in the order the algorithm executes them.
121.explanation: Following the actual execution order is essential to tracing a program.

122.statement: Validation proves that a user's data is factually correct.
122.explanation: Validation checks whether input satisfies defined rules, not whether it is true.
122.correction: Validation checks whether input satisfies defined rules, not whether it is true.

123.statement: A development method should be selected using the project's requirements and constraints.
123.explanation: Risk, deadlines and changing requirements affect which approach fits.

124.statement: Procedural and object-oriented programming organise code in exactly the same way.
124.explanation: Procedural code centres on procedures; OOP organises state and behaviour in objects.
124.correction: Procedural code centres on procedures; OOP organises state and behaviour in objects.

125.statement: A procedural program can use modules to separate related tasks.
125.explanation: Modularity reduces duplication and makes code easier to maintain.

126.statement: In LMC, an instruction's operand can never identify a memory address.
126.explanation: Many LMC instructions use an address to access a memory location.
126.correction: Many LMC instructions use an address to access a memory location.

127.statement: Immediate addressing uses a value contained in the instruction itself.
127.explanation: Direct addressing instead supplies an address of the operand.

128.statement: Lossy compression always allows perfect recovery of the original file.
128.explanation: Lossless compression is reversible exactly; lossy compression discards information.
128.correction: Lossless compression is reversible exactly; lossy compression discards information.

129.statement: Run-length encoding can represent a repeated run by storing a value and a count.
129.explanation: Long runs may compress well but short alternating sequences may not.

130.statement: Dictionary compression requires every repeated substring to be stored in full each time.
130.explanation: References to dictionary entries can replace repeated sequences.
130.correction: References to dictionary entries can replace repeated sequences.

131.statement: Symmetric encryption uses the same shared secret key for encryption and decryption.
131.explanation: Both parties need secure access to the key.

132.statement: A public key in asymmetric encryption must always be kept secret.
132.explanation: The public key can be shared; the private key must be protected.
132.correction: The public key can be shared; the private key must be protected.

133.statement: Hybrid encryption can use public-key techniques to establish a symmetric session key.
133.explanation: Fast symmetric encryption then protects the bulk data.

134.statement: A cryptographic hash is designed to be decrypted back to the original message.
134.explanation: A hash is one-way; encryption is designed to be reversible with a key.
134.correction: A hash is one-way; encryption is designed to be reversible with a key.

135.statement: A primary key uniquely identifies a row in a relational database table.

136.statement: A many-to-many relationship can always be implemented using just one foreign key in one of the two tables.
136.explanation: A linking table is normally used to represent many-to-many relationships.
136.correction: A linking table is normally used to represent many-to-many relationships.

137.statement: Second Normal Form removes partial dependencies on part of a composite key.
137.explanation: It builds on First Normal Form to reduce redundancy.

138.statement: Third Normal Form permits non-key attributes to depend on other non-key attributes.
138.explanation: 3NF removes transitive dependencies of non-key attributes.
138.correction: 3NF removes transitive dependencies of non-key attributes.

139.statement: A SQL JOIN can combine rows from related tables using a matching condition.
139.explanation: It supports retrieving fields stored in separate tables.

140.statement: A DELETE statement without a WHERE clause necessarily removes only one selected row.
140.explanation: Without a filter, DELETE can remove every row in the table.
140.correction: Without a filter, DELETE can remove every row in the table.

141.statement: Referential integrity helps stop foreign keys referring to nonexistent records.
141.explanation: A valid reference should point to an existing primary or unique key.

142.statement: The ACID property Atomicity means a transaction can be only half completed.

143.statement: A WAN connects networks across a wider geographical area than a typical LAN.
143.explanation: A LAN normally serves a local site; a WAN spans larger distances.

144.statement: At the network layer, IP is responsible for drawing the contents of a web page.
144.explanation: IP handles addressing and routing packets; the application handles page content.
144.correction: IP handles addressing and routing packets; the application handles page content.

145.statement: DNS can resolve a domain name to an IP address used to route traffic.
145.explanation: A name lookup helps identify a network destination.

146.statement: Packet switching requires a dedicated end-to-end circuit throughout a transfer.
146.explanation: Packets can share network links and travel independently.
146.correction: Packets can share network links and travel independently.

147.statement: A phishing attack can trick someone into revealing credentials.
147.explanation: It relies on deceptive messages or pages rather than legitimate authorisation.

148.statement: A firewall guarantees that every malicious message will be detected and blocked.
148.explanation: A firewall applies rules; layered security is still necessary.
148.correction: A firewall applies rules; layered security is still necessary.

149.statement: A router forwards traffic between networks, while a switch forwards frames within a LAN.
149.explanation: They operate at different points in network communication.

150.statement: In a peer-to-peer model every service must be controlled by one dedicated central server.
150.explanation: Peers can share resources directly without a dedicated server.
150.correction: Peers can share resources directly without a dedicated server.

151.statement: An HTML form can contain labelled input elements for users to enter data.
151.explanation: Semantic markup helps structure forms and make them accessible.

152.statement: In CSS, an element's padding is outside its border.
152.explanation: Padding lies between content and border; margin is outside the border.
152.correction: Padding lies between content and border; margin is outside the border.

153.statement: JavaScript event handlers can respond to a user's interaction with a page.
153.explanation: For example, a click handler can update the DOM.

154.statement: Client-side form validation makes server-side validation unnecessary.
154.explanation: Server-side checks remain necessary because client-side checks can be bypassed.
154.correction: Server-side checks remain necessary because client-side checks can be bypassed.

155.statement: Search engines use crawlers to discover pages before indexing their content.
155.explanation: Crawling finds pages; indexing organises information for retrieval.

156.statement: PageRank estimates a page's importance using only the number of words on it.
156.explanation: PageRank uses links between pages to derive an importance score.
156.correction: PageRank uses links between pages to derive an importance score.

157.statement: Server-side processing runs on a server rather than in the user's browser.
157.explanation: The server can apply logic and send a result back to the client.

158.statement: Data protection rules permit unrestricted use of any personal data collected.
158.explanation: Organisations must use personal data on an appropriate lawful basis and follow applicable rules.
158.correction: Organisations must use personal data on an appropriate lawful basis and follow applicable rules.

159.statement: The Computer Misuse Act includes offences involving unauthorised access.
159.explanation: Access without authorisation may be a criminal offence.

160.statement: Crediting the creator always grants permission to copy copyrighted software.
160.explanation: Attribution does not automatically provide a licence or legal exception.
160.correction: Attribution does not automatically provide a licence or legal exception.

181.statement: Binary search requires sorted data before it can safely discard half of a search interval.
181.explanation: Year 13 starting diagnostic revisiting previously taught Year 12 algorithms.
181.exceptionReason: Year 13 course entry: prior Year 12 algorithm knowledge

182.statement: A recursive algorithm never needs a base case.
182.explanation: A base case stops the recursive calls.
182.correction: A base case stops the recursive calls.

183.statement: Nested recursive calls return in the reverse order from which they were entered.
183.explanation: The call stack unwinds after the base case.

184.statement: A recursive function can be debugged without checking its base case.
184.explanation: An incorrect or unreachable base case can cause non-termination or wrong answers.
184.correction: An incorrect or unreachable base case can cause non-termination or wrong answers.

185.statement: Ascending bubble sort moves the largest remaining value towards the end after a complete pass.

186.statement: Insertion sort always starts a new sorted list from scratch for every element.
186.explanation: It grows an existing sorted prefix by inserting the next element.
186.correction: It grows an existing sorted prefix by inserting the next element.

187.statement: Merge sort combines already-sorted sublists into a larger sorted list.
187.explanation: It repeatedly selects the next smallest available element for ascending order.

188.statement: Linear search requires the list to be sorted first.
188.explanation: Linear search checks elements in turn and works on unsorted data.
188.correction: Linear search checks elements in turn and works on unsorted data.

189.statement: Binary search repeatedly narrows a sorted list's search interval.
189.explanation: The midpoint comparison determines the interval to keep.

190.statement: An O(n) search generally grows more slowly than an O(log n) search for large n.
190.explanation: Logarithmic growth is slower than linear growth.
190.correction: Logarithmic growth is slower than linear growth.

191.statement: A local variable normally cannot be accessed outside the scope where it was declared.
191.explanation: Scope determines which code can use the variable.

192.statement: A function that returns a value and a procedure that does not are identical in their return behaviour.
192.explanation: A function returns a result; a procedure-style routine does not.
192.correction: A function returns a result; a procedure-style routine does not.

193.statement: Passing a variable by reference can allow a subroutine to change the caller's variable.
193.explanation: By value instead provides a copy of the value.

194.statement: An arithmetic right shift of a negative two's-complement value always fills left positions with zeros.
194.explanation: An arithmetic right shift preserves the sign bit, filling with ones for a negative number.
194.correction: An arithmetic right shift preserves the sign bit, filling with ones for a negative number.

195.statement: In normalised positive two's-complement floating point, the mantissa starts with 01.
195.explanation: The leading bits differ for negative normalised mantissas.

196.statement: Two floating-point mantissas with unequal exponents can be added without alignment.
196.explanation: Align exponents first so corresponding binary positions have the same value.
196.correction: Align exponents first so corresponding binary positions have the same value.

197.statement: A record can group named fields of different types.
197.explanation: Records differ from homogeneous arrays and positional tuples.

198.statement: A queue removes the last item inserted before older items.
198.explanation: FIFO queues remove the earliest inserted item first.
198.correction: FIFO queues remove the earliest inserted item first.

199.statement: A linked-list node can store data together with a reference to another node.
199.explanation: References connect nodes and allow traversal.

200.statement: In a binary search tree, values smaller than a node are always stored to its right.
200.explanation: Standard BST ordering puts smaller values to the left.
200.correction: Standard BST ordering puts smaller values to the left.

201.statement: An adjacency list records which vertices connect to each vertex in a graph.
201.explanation: It represents graph edges using each vertex's neighbours.

202.statement: Two different keys can never map to the same hash value.
202.explanation: A hash collision occurs when different keys share a bucket or hash.
202.correction: A hash collision occurs when different keys share a bucket or hash.

203.statement: De Morgan's law transforms NOT (A OR B) into (NOT A) AND (NOT B).
203.explanation: Negation distributes across OR while changing it to AND.

204.statement: A Karnaugh-map group of four 1s must retain every variable in the resulting term.
204.explanation: Variables that change inside a valid group can be eliminated.
204.correction: Variables that change inside a valid group can be eliminated.

205.statement: A full adder produces a sum bit and a carry-out bit.
205.explanation: It adds two data bits and a carry-in.

206.statement: The execution order of assignments is irrelevant when tracing an unfamiliar algorithm.
206.explanation: Each assignment may change values used by later instructions.
206.correction: Each assignment may change values used by later instructions.

207.statement: Choosing between a stack and a queue depends on the required removal order.
207.explanation: Stacks are LIFO; queues are FIFO.

208.statement: An algorithm with O(n²) growth will normally scale better than O(n) for very large inputs.
208.explanation: Quadratic growth increases faster than linear growth.
208.correction: Quadratic growth increases faster than linear growth.

209.statement: A synoptic program can combine loops, conditions and data structures in one solution.
209.explanation: Correct solutions often need several programming techniques together.

210.statement: For raw image data, increasing colour depth always decreases the required file size.
210.explanation: More bits per pixel increase uncompressed size for the same dimensions.
210.correction: More bits per pixel increase uncompressed size for the same dimensions.

211.statement: Debugging should identify the incorrect step and test the corrected version.
211.explanation: A fix needs evidence that the behaviour is now as expected.

212.statement: A stack removes the oldest item first, while a queue removes the newest.
212.explanation: Stacks are LIFO; queues are FIFO.
212.correction: Stacks are LIFO; queues are FIFO.

213.statement: Tracing an algorithm means updating the values in the order its instructions execute.
213.explanation: This supports accurate Paper 2 exam answers.

214.statement: A negative two's-complement number always starts with a zero sign bit.
214.explanation: The highest bit is 1 for negative two's-complement values.
214.correction: The highest bit is 1 for negative two's-complement values.

215.statement: Assessment feedback should link an incorrect answer to a corrected method or idea.
215.explanation: Explaining the correction supports future improvement.

216.statement: A corrected examination answer needs only the final number and never the working.
216.explanation: Clear method and reasoning show what has been improved.
216.correction: Clear method and reasoning show what has been improved.

217.statement: Quicksort uses a pivot to partition values into appropriate regions.
217.explanation: Partitioning separates elements for the subsequent sorting work.

218.statement: After a quicksort partition, the entire array must already be completely sorted.
218.explanation: A partition positions values around a pivot; further partitions may be needed.
218.correction: A partition positions values around a pivot; further partitions may be needed.

219.statement: Dijkstra's algorithm finds shortest paths under the usual non-negative-edge condition.
219.explanation: Its greedy choice is valid for non-negative edge weights.

220.statement: Dijkstra's algorithm can safely treat an unvisited node with the largest tentative distance as the next shortest.
220.explanation: It selects the smallest tentative distance among unvisited candidates.
220.correction: It selects the smallest tentative distance among unvisited candidates.

221.statement: In A* search, f(n) = g(n) + h(n).
221.explanation: g is known cost so far; h estimates remaining cost.

222.statement: A* is guaranteed to find an optimal route with any arbitrary overestimating heuristic.
222.explanation: Optimality requires suitable heuristic conditions, such as admissibility in standard settings.
222.correction: Optimality requires suitable heuristic conditions, such as admissibility in standard settings.

223.statement: Algorithm choice should explain requirements and preconditions, not merely name the method.
223.explanation: For example, binary search needs sorted data.

224.statement: A linked list implemented with object references must store every node contiguously.
224.explanation: References connect nodes independently of their memory positions.
224.correction: References connect nodes independently of their memory positions.

225.statement: Inserting a smaller value into a binary search tree follows a left link from the comparison node.
225.explanation: Standard BST ordering places smaller values in the left subtree.

226.statement: Testing an object-oriented program requires checking only a class's constructor.
226.explanation: Methods, state changes and interactions also need tests.
226.correction: Methods, state changes and interactions also need tests.

227.statement: Post-order tree traversal visits a node after visiting its descendants.
227.explanation: In a binary tree the usual sequence is left, right, root.

228.statement: An IDE's debugger can only show final output and cannot pause execution.
228.explanation: Debuggers support breakpoints, stepping and inspecting variables.
228.correction: Debuggers support breakpoints, stepping and inspecting variables.

229.statement: A synoptic OOP solution may need classes, objects, methods and justified relationships.
229.explanation: The model should link its design to the problem.

230.statement: Functional, procedural and object-oriented paradigms always structure programs identically.
230.explanation: They organise state and computation in different ways.
230.correction: They organise state and computation in different ways.

231.statement: A comparison of programming paradigms should consider their suitability for the task.
231.explanation: Different paradigms can make some problems easier to express or maintain.

232.statement: A local variable is automatically available to every subroutine in a program.
232.explanation: Local scope limits access; values can be passed as parameters.
232.correction: Local scope limits access; values can be passed as parameters.

233.statement: An algorithm written in OCR pseudocode can use file operations and clear control structures.
233.explanation: Pseudocode describes logic without depending on a full implementation language.

234.statement: Waterfall and Agile both require all requirements to be fixed before development starts.
234.explanation: Agile methods allow iterative feedback and changed priorities.
234.correction: Agile methods allow iterative feedback and changed priorities.

235.statement: The Spiral model explicitly considers risk during repeated development cycles.
235.explanation: Risk assessment helps determine what to build and test next.

236.statement: A successful normal test proves that a program handles all invalid inputs.
236.explanation: Separate boundary and invalid tests are still necessary.
236.correction: Separate boundary and invalid tests are still necessary.

237.statement: Documenting an algorithm should make its steps and decisions clear enough to trace.
237.explanation: Clear pseudocode supports understanding and checking behaviour.

238.statement: A program that passes one test has demonstrated correctness for every possible input.
238.explanation: A broader selection of cases is needed, and testing cannot prove every case.
238.correction: A broader selection of cases is needed, and testing cannot prove every case.

239.statement: An abstraction leaves out details that do not affect the intended solution.
239.explanation: A useful model keeps the properties necessary for its purpose.

240.statement: A precondition is something that should be checked only after an algorithm has finished.
240.explanation: A precondition must hold before the operation begins.
240.correction: A precondition must hold before the operation begins.

241.statement: Retesting after fixing a fault helps check whether the correction worked.
241.explanation: It should also check that the change has not caused another fault.

242.statement: Procedural thinking means the order of subroutines can never affect the result.
242.explanation: Dependencies and sequencing between subroutines may matter.
242.correction: Dependencies and sequencing between subroutines may matter.

243.statement: A logical condition can select different execution paths in an algorithm.

244.statement: In the processor, the Memory Address Register stores the data just read from memory.
244.explanation: MAR stores an address; MDR stores transferred data.
244.correction: MAR stores an address; MDR stores transferred data.

245.statement: Tasks can run concurrently when their dependencies permit overlapping progress.
245.explanation: Concurrency does not always require simultaneous physical execution.

246.statement: Selecting a development method depends only on the programmer's favourite method.
246.explanation: Requirements, risks, team size and deadlines affect the choice.
246.correction: Requirements, risks, team size and deadlines affect the choice.

247.statement: A computational problem is easier to specify when inputs, constraints and outcomes are clear.
247.explanation: A precise problem statement enables a testable algorithm.

248.statement: A binary search can safely ignore the sorted-data requirement.
248.explanation: The midpoint decision relies on ordering.
248.correction: The midpoint decision relies on ordering.

249.statement: Improving an answer after mock feedback should include explaining the correct method.
249.explanation: A corrected explanation demonstrates the misunderstanding has been addressed.

250.statement: O(log n) algorithms always require more steps than O(n) algorithms as inputs become large.
250.explanation: Logarithmic growth is slower asymptotically than linear growth.
250.correction: Logarithmic growth is slower asymptotically than linear growth.

251.statement: A synoptic assessment review should identify which knowledge or method needs improvement.
251.explanation: Targeted reteaching follows evidence from responses.

252.statement: The ALU holds the address of the next instruction to fetch.
252.explanation: The Program Counter holds that address; the ALU performs arithmetic and logic.
252.correction: The Program Counter holds that address; the ALU performs arithmetic and logic.

253.statement: The address bus carries the location of memory being accessed.
253.explanation: The data bus carries the values transferred.

254.statement: Adding more cache always guarantees exactly twice the speed.
254.explanation: Performance depends on memory access patterns and other processor factors.
254.correction: Performance depends on memory access patterns and other processor factors.

255.statement: Harvard architecture separates instruction and data paths.
255.explanation: Von Neumann designs normally share the main instruction/data memory space.

256.statement: CISC always means every instruction takes exactly one clock cycle.
256.explanation: Instruction costs differ; CISC and RISC describe instruction-set design philosophies.
256.correction: Instruction costs differ; CISC and RISC describe instruction-set design philosophies.

257.statement: A GPU can process many similar operations in parallel.
257.explanation: It is especially useful for suitable high-throughput workloads.

258.statement: A printer is normally an input device because it receives data from a computer.
258.explanation: A printer produces output on paper.
258.correction: A printer produces output on paper.

259.statement: Choosing hardware in an exam answer should be justified using the task's demands.
259.explanation: Suitability depends on performance, memory, cost or physical context.

260.statement: Magnetic hard disks store data using flash memory cells without moving parts.
260.explanation: HDDs store data magnetically on spinning platters.
260.correction: HDDs store data magnetically on spinning platters.

261.statement: Virtual memory uses secondary storage to supplement available RAM.
261.explanation: It is slower than physical RAM but can hold pages not currently in RAM.

262.statement: Immediate addressing always reads an operand from the memory location in the instruction.
262.explanation: Immediate addressing uses the literal value encoded in the instruction.
262.correction: Immediate addressing uses the literal value encoded in the instruction.

263.statement: The LMC accumulator holds values used by arithmetic instructions.
263.explanation: ADD and SUB update the accumulator using operands.

264.statement: An unconditional LMC branch executes only if the accumulator is zero.
264.explanation: BRA always changes the next instruction to the target address.
264.correction: BRA always changes the next instruction to the target address.

265.statement: An operating system manages processes, memory and input/output resources.

266.statement: An OS cannot respond to an interrupt while another user program is running.
266.explanation: Interrupts allow hardware or system events to gain attention.
266.correction: Interrupts allow hardware or system events to gain attention.

267.statement: Paging divides memory into fixed-size pages and frames.
267.explanation: Pages need not map to contiguous physical memory.

268.statement: An interrupt service routine runs only after the whole operating system shuts down.
268.explanation: It responds to an interrupt while the system is operating.
268.correction: It responds to an interrupt while the system is operating.

269.statement: Round Robin scheduling gives ready processes a time slice in turn.
269.explanation: An unfinished process can return to the ready queue.

270.statement: All operating systems must provide a graphical user interface.
270.explanation: Some systems use a command-line interface or run without a GUI.
270.correction: Some systems use a command-line interface or run without a GUI.

271.statement: A device driver provides an interface between the OS and hardware.
271.explanation: Drivers let the system operate particular devices.

272.statement: Utility software and application software always have exactly the same purpose.
272.explanation: Utilities maintain or manage systems; applications serve user tasks.
272.correction: Utilities maintain or manage systems; applications serve user tasks.

273.statement: A SQL WHERE clause can restrict which rows are returned.
273.explanation: It applies a condition to filter records.

274.statement: An interpreter always creates a standalone machine-code executable before running any statement.
274.explanation: An interpreter can translate and execute code incrementally.
274.correction: An interpreter can translate and execute code incrementally.

275.statement: A linker resolves references between compiled program modules.
275.explanation: It combines code and libraries needed to build a program.

276.statement: A primary key may contain duplicate values whenever records share a name.
276.explanation: Primary-key values must uniquely identify records.
276.correction: Primary-key values must uniquely identify records.

277.statement: An entity relationship diagram can show one-to-many relationships between entities.
277.explanation: A cardinality label indicates how many related records can exist.

278.statement: Third Normal Form deliberately keeps transitive dependencies between non-key attributes.
278.explanation: 3NF removes such dependencies to reduce update anomalies.
278.correction: 3NF removes such dependencies to reduce update anomalies.

279.statement: SQL JOIN can combine related data held in separate tables.
279.explanation: A joining condition links matching rows.

280.statement: SQL DROP removes just the rows matching a WHERE condition.
280.explanation: DROP removes a database object such as a table; DELETE removes rows.
280.correction: DROP removes a database object such as a table; DELETE removes rows.

281.statement: Assessment feedback on a data topic should identify a corrected method or misconception.
281.explanation: The aim is to improve the next response, not just record a mark.

282.statement: A transaction with ACID Atomicity may save only half its changes and still succeed.

283.statement: A router connects networks, whereas a switch commonly connects devices within a LAN.
283.explanation: Their roles differ in forwarding across or within networks.

284.statement: DNS is primarily responsible for encrypting the contents of a web request.
284.explanation: DNS resolves names to records such as IP addresses.
284.correction: DNS resolves names to records such as IP addresses.

285.statement: Packet switching allows packets from different communications to share network links.
285.explanation: Packets are routed through a shared network.

286.statement: A firewall guarantees protection against every kind of phishing or malware.
286.explanation: Firewalls are one layer of network security, not a complete defence.
286.correction: Firewalls are one layer of network security, not a complete defence.

287.statement: Lossless compression can reconstruct the original data exactly.
287.explanation: Lossy methods discard information and cannot generally restore every bit.

288.statement: Run-length encoding is always shorter than the original data even with no repeated values.
288.explanation: Runs that are too short may make RLE ineffective or larger.
288.correction: Runs that are too short may make RLE ineffective or larger.

289.statement: Asymmetric encryption uses a public and private key pair.
289.explanation: The private key is kept secret; the public key can be distributed.

290.statement: A cryptographic hash is designed to be reversible using a decryption key.
290.explanation: Hashing is one-way and is not the same as encryption.
290.correction: Hashing is one-way and is not the same as encryption.

291.statement: A misconception check is useful when it explains why a tempting answer is wrong.
291.explanation: Correcting the reasoning strengthens later retrieval.

292.statement: An HTML form can never contain labels for its input controls.
292.explanation: Associated labels improve usability and accessibility.
292.correction: Associated labels improve usability and accessibility.

293.statement: JavaScript can update a page in response to an event while CSS controls its presentation.
293.explanation: They have different roles within a web interface.

294.statement: Server-side code always runs inside the visitor's web browser.
294.explanation: Server-side code executes on the server.
294.correction: Server-side code executes on the server.

295.statement: A search-engine index organises information discovered by crawling.
295.explanation: It allows relevant content to be retrieved without recrawling every page per search.

296.statement: The Computer Misuse Act and data-protection law regulate precisely the same offences.
296.explanation: They address different concerns, including unauthorised access and lawful processing of personal data.
296.correction: They address different concerns, including unauthorised access and lawful processing of personal data.

297.statement: An automated decision system can affect people unfairly if its data or rules are biased.
297.explanation: Fairness, transparency and privacy are important considerations.

298.statement: Digital accessibility matters only to people who are completely unable to see a screen.
298.explanation: Accessible design benefits users with many different needs.
298.correction: Accessible design benefits users with many different needs.

299.statement: Backtracking can undo a failed choice and explore another branch.
299.explanation: It returns to a previous decision point after a dead end.

300.statement: An apparent correlation in a data visualisation always proves causation.
300.explanation: Correlation does not establish a causal relationship.
300.correction: Correlation does not establish a causal relationship.

301.statement: A heuristic can guide a search without guaranteeing the best possible solution.
301.explanation: It estimates promising choices to save work.

302.statement: An O(n²) algorithm scales more slowly than O(n log n) for sufficiently large n.

303.statement: Tracing unfamiliar code involves following the actual order of execution.
303.explanation: Each state change must be applied before the next dependent step.

304.statement: OCR pseudocode can ignore assignment and comparison syntax because they mean exactly the same thing.
304.explanation: Assignment changes a value; comparison checks a condition.
304.correction: Assignment changes a value; comparison checks a condition.

305.statement: A final specification check should identify any topic or technique that still needs practice.
305.explanation: This supports targeted revision before assessments.

306.statement: After a synoptic assessment, a learner can improve only by memorising the final answers.
306.explanation: Correcting methods and explaining misconceptions is more useful.
306.correction: Correcting methods and explaining misconceptions is more useful.

307.statement: Paper 1 processor questions can require distinguishing the MAR from the MDR.
307.explanation: MAR holds an address; MDR holds data being transferred.

308.statement: A corrected Paper 1 explanation needs no reason linking a feature to its effect.
308.explanation: Exam explanations should connect an accurate point to its consequence.
308.correction: Exam explanations should connect an accurate point to its consequence.

309.statement: Paper 2 trace tables should reflect variable updates in the algorithm's execution order.
309.explanation: Later values can depend on earlier changes.

310.statement: A Paper 2 correction is complete if it changes the final output without fixing the flawed method.
310.explanation: The method must be corrected so it works for relevant cases.
310.correction: The method must be corrected so it works for relevant cases.

311.statement: A recursive function needs a reachable base case to terminate.
311.explanation: Without one, recursive calls may continue indefinitely.

312.statement: When tracing unfamiliar code, variable assignments may be rearranged alphabetically.
312.explanation: Values must be updated in the order statements execute.
312.correction: Values must be updated in the order statements execute.

313.statement: To add floating-point binary values, the exponents must first be aligned.
313.explanation: Corresponding mantissa bit positions need equal place values.

314.statement: The CPU's Memory Data Register stores the address of the next instruction to fetch.
314.explanation: The Program Counter holds the next address; MDR carries transferred data.
314.correction: The Program Counter holds the next address; MDR carries transferred data.

315.statement: A SQL WHERE clause filters rows based on a condition.
315.explanation: A query can combine it with SELECT and other clauses.

316.statement: A network firewall replaces the need for encryption when protecting confidential data.
316.explanation: Encryption and firewall rules serve different, complementary purposes.
316.correction: Encryption and firewall rules serve different, complementary purposes.

317.statement: A strong extended response explains why a computer-system feature is suitable for its scenario.

318.statement: A Paper 2 extended response needs only pseudocode with no explanation of algorithm choice.
318.explanation: The question may also require justified decisions or complexity discussion.
318.correction: The question may also require justified decisions or complexity discussion.

319.statement: Targeted Paper 1 reteaching should address the specific misconception shown by earlier work.
319.explanation: Correcting a cause is more useful than repeating an answer.

320.statement: Paper 2 reteaching is complete when a learner copies the worked answer without testing a new case.
320.explanation: Independent application to a new problem checks whether the method was learned.
320.correction: Independent application to a new problem checks whether the method was learned.

001.statement: A whole-number count is suitably stored as an integer rather than a real number.
001.explanation: An integer represents whole numbers; this is a GCSE diagnostic before H446 begins.

002.statement: An unsigned eight-bit binary value can represent −1.
002.explanation: Unsigned eight-bit values range from 0 to 255.
002.correction: Unsigned eight-bit values range from 0 to 255.

003.explanation: The most significant bit is worth −128; the other seven bits total 127.

004.statement: A logical right shift discards the leftmost bit.
004.explanation: A right shift discards the rightmost bit and moves the remaining bits right.
004.correction: A right shift discards the rightmost bit and moves the remaining bits right.

005.statement: A positive normalised two's-complement binary mantissa begins 01.
005.explanation: In the H446 convention a positive normalised mantissa starts 0.1 in binary.

006.statement: A floating-point exponent is added to the mantissa to obtain the stored value.
006.explanation: The value is the mantissa multiplied by 2 raised to the exponent.
006.correction: The value is the mantissa multiplied by 2 raised to the exponent.

007.statement: Two floating-point mantissas should be aligned to the same exponent before addition.
007.explanation: Matching exponents makes their binary place values line up.

008.statement: Floating-point subtraction can directly combine mantissas with different exponents.
008.explanation: The exponents must first be aligned, then the mantissas can be subtracted.
008.correction: The exponents must first be aligned, then the mantissas can be subtracted.

009.statement: Unicode represents a wider range of writing systems than standard ASCII.
009.explanation: ASCII has a small character set; Unicode supports many languages and symbols.

010.statement: In C#, both branches of an if–else statement execute on every run.
010.explanation: Only the branch selected by the condition executes.
010.correction: Only the branch selected by the condition executes.

011.statement: A while loop can repeat until its condition becomes false.
011.explanation: The condition controls whether another iteration runs.

012.statement: A C# method declared void returns a value to the caller.
012.explanation: A void method has no return value.
012.correction: A void method has no return value.

013.statement: A local variable is normally accessible only inside its declaring scope.
013.explanation: Scope limits where a variable can be read or changed.

014.statement: In a sequence of instructions, their execution order cannot change the outcome.
014.explanation: Statements in sequence run in order; changing that order may change state.
014.correction: Statements in sequence run in order; changing that order may change state.

015.statement: A loop can redraw a noughts-and-crosses board after each turn.
015.explanation: Iteration avoids writing the same board-display steps repeatedly.

016.statement: In the modelled MakeMove() method, a successful move returns false.
016.explanation: A successful move returns true; false indicates failure.
016.correction: A successful move returns true; false indicates failure.

017.statement: A valid move in a turn-based game should update the board's stored state.
017.explanation: The new state allows subsequent turns and win checks to use the updated board.

018.statement: The first item in a zero-indexed C# array is accessed with index 1.
018.explanation: The first array element has index 0.
018.correction: The first array element has index 0.

019.statement: A record can group related fields that have different data types.
019.explanation: For example, an item may have a string name and an integer count.

020.statement: Following pointers in a linked list always requires consecutive array positions.
020.explanation: Nodes are followed using their links, not necessarily neighbouring physical positions.
020.correction: Nodes are followed using their links, not necessarily neighbouring physical positions.

021.statement: A queue removes the most recently added item first.
021.explanation: A queue uses first-in, first-out; a stack uses last-in, first-out.
021.correction: A queue uses first-in, first-out; a stack uses last-in, first-out.

022.statement: An edge in a directed graph has a specified direction.
022.explanation: A→B does not automatically imply an edge B→A.

023.statement: In a binary search tree, values smaller than a node are placed in its right subtree.
023.explanation: Smaller values go left; larger values go right under the standard ordering rule.
023.correction: Smaller values go left; larger values go right under the standard ordering rule.

024.statement: Two different keys can produce the same hash-table bucket.
024.explanation: This is a collision, which needs a defined handling method.

025.statement: The best data structure is always the one that uses the least memory.
025.explanation: The required operations, access patterns, speed and memory all affect the choice.
025.correction: The required operations, access patterns, speed and memory all affect the choice.

026.statement: Binary search relies on the search data being sorted.
026.explanation: Ordering makes it valid to discard half of the remaining search range.

027.statement: An AND gate outputs 1 whenever either input is 1.
027.explanation: AND outputs 1 only when both inputs are 1.
027.correction: AND outputs 1 only when both inputs are 1.

028.statement: De Morgan's law gives NOT (A AND B) = (NOT A) OR (NOT B).
028.explanation: Negating an AND changes it to OR with each input negated.

029.statement: Horizontally or vertically adjacent Karnaugh-map cells differ in one input bit.
029.explanation: This allows a changing variable to be eliminated when adjacent 1s are grouped.

030.statement: Grouping four adjacent 1s in a Karnaugh map always retains every input variable.
030.explanation: Variables that change within a valid group are removed from the simplified term.
030.correction: Variables that change within a valid group are removed from the simplified term.

031.statement: A full adder includes a carry-in as well as the two main input bits.
031.explanation: It produces a sum bit and a carry-out bit.

032.statement: A rising-edge D-type flip-flop changes Q continuously whenever D changes.
032.explanation: It samples D on the active clock edge and holds Q between clock events.
032.correction: It samples D on the active clock edge and holds Q between clock events.

033.statement: A login routine can validate that a username is not empty before checking credentials.
033.explanation: Input validation can reject a blank username before authentication logic runs.

034.statement: Linear probing must stop permanently when a collision occurs in the final bucket.
034.explanation: Probing can wrap to bucket 0 when searching for another available location.
034.correction: Probing can wrap to bucket 0 when searching for another available location.

035.statement: Testing a completed login project should include invalid as well as valid inputs.
035.explanation: Invalid-input cases can expose faults missed by successful login tests.

036.statement: Showing the steps of a calculation can reveal an error even when its final answer is wrong.
036.explanation: Working makes methods checkable and can support method marks in an exam.

037.statement: A useful revision mind-map branch consists only of an unexplained topic heading.
037.explanation: A strong branch also includes an example or method, misconception and labelled link.
037.correction: A strong branch also includes an example or method, misconception and labelled link.

038.statement: Binary search requires an appropriately ordered collection.
038.explanation: This was covered when the mind map connected algorithms with data structures.

039.statement: An object is a blueprint from which classes are created.
039.explanation: A class is the blueprint; an object is an instance.
039.correction: A class is the blueprint; an object is an instance.

040.statement: An object's method can change values stored in its attributes.
040.explanation: For example, an attack method can reduce another object's HP.

041.statement: A constructor can give a newly created object its initial attribute values.
041.explanation: Constructor code runs during object creation and sets initial state.

042.statement: Keeping a field private allows any outside code to change it directly.
042.explanation: Private access helps encapsulate state; controlled methods may manage changes.
042.correction: Private access helps encapsulate state; controlled methods may manage changes.

043.statement: A derived class can inherit accessible members of its base class.

044.statement: An overridden virtual method always runs the base-class implementation.
044.explanation: Dynamic dispatch can choose the derived class's override.
044.correction: Dynamic dispatch can choose the derived class's override.

045.statement: A Student borrowing a Book is normally an inheritance relationship.
045.explanation: Borrowing is an association: a Student is not a kind of Book.
045.correction: Borrowing is an association: a Student is not a kind of Book.

046.statement: A class-model answer should justify whether an object relationship is inheritance or association.
046.explanation: The relationship depends on whether it is an is-a or other connection.

047.statement: A C# array can store references to multiple objects of a class.
047.explanation: Each indexed element can refer to an object.

048.statement: A two-dimensional C# array needs only one index to select a specific cell.
048.explanation: Two indices identify the row and column.
048.correction: Two indices identify the row and column.

049.statement: List<T>.RemoveAt removes the first element equal to a given value.
049.explanation: RemoveAt uses an index; Remove matches a value.
049.correction: RemoveAt uses an index; Remove matches a value.

050.statement: Stack<T>.Pop removes the current top item.

051.statement: A queue serves elements in first-in, first-out order.
051.explanation: Dequeue removes the element waiting at the front.

052.statement: Every node of a linked list must occupy the next memory address after its predecessor.
052.explanation: Nodes are connected by references, not required to be consecutive in memory.
052.correction: Nodes are connected by references, not required to be consecutive in memory.

053.statement: In a binary search tree, values smaller than a node belong to its left subtree.
053.explanation: This ordering supports efficient directed searches in suitable trees.

054.statement: Breadth-first traversal of a graph typically uses a queue.
054.explanation: FIFO order supports visiting nodes level by level.

055.statement: A hash collision proves that two keys are identical.
055.explanation: Different keys can map to the same hash bucket.
055.correction: Different keys can map to the same hash bucket.

056.statement: A stack is the most suitable structure when customers must be served in arrival order.
056.explanation: A FIFO queue preserves arrival order.
056.correction: A FIFO queue preserves arrival order.

057.statement: Post-order tree traversal visits a node's children before the node itself.
057.explanation: For a binary tree the typical order is left, right, root.

058.statement: A constructor can initialise fields when a LibraryLoan object is created.
058.explanation: The constructor establishes the object's starting state.

059.statement: An exam answer choosing a data structure needs only its name, never a justification.
059.explanation: The required operations and scenario should justify the choice.
059.correction: The required operations and scenario should justify the choice.

060.statement: Abstraction removes irrelevant details while retaining information needed for the model.
060.explanation: The chosen model should preserve relevant behaviour and constraints.

061.statement: Refining an abstraction means including every real-world detail, even if irrelevant.
061.explanation: A model retains useful details and makes its simplifying assumptions explicit.
061.correction: A model retains useful details and makes its simplifying assumptions explicit.

062.statement: A precondition states something that must hold before an operation can work correctly.
062.explanation: It is checked before relying on the operation.

063.statement: Procedural thinking means the steps of a solution may be executed in any order.
063.explanation: The order and dependencies of subtasks matter.
063.correction: The order and dependencies of subtasks matter.

064.statement: A Boolean condition can control which branch of an algorithm executes.
064.explanation: The condition evaluates to true or false.

065.statement: Two tasks are independent when one must wait for the other's output.
065.explanation: Independent tasks do not require that dependency before progressing.
065.correction: Independent tasks do not require that dependency before progressing.

066.statement: A computational problem needs identifiable inputs, constraints and an assessable outcome.
066.explanation: These features help define a problem that an algorithm can solve.

067.statement: Decomposition combines every subproblem into one unmanageable task.
067.explanation: It divides a problem into smaller, more manageable parts.
067.correction: It divides a problem into smaller, more manageable parts.

068.statement: Divide and conquer solves smaller subproblems and combines their results.
068.explanation: The overall solution is built from solutions to the divided problems.

069.statement: Backtracking must keep exploring a branch after it has been shown invalid.
069.explanation: It can undo a choice and return to an earlier decision point.
069.correction: It can undo a choice and return to an earlier decision point.

070.statement: A correlation found during data mining proves that one variable causes another.
070.explanation: Correlation is an association and does not establish causation.
070.correction: Correlation is an association and does not establish causation.

071.statement: A heuristic guides a search without guaranteeing an optimal answer in every case.
071.explanation: It is a practical estimate or rule of thumb.

072.statement: Pipelining requires one task to finish every stage before the next task starts.
072.explanation: Different stages can work on different tasks concurrently.
072.correction: Different stages can work on different tasks concurrently.

073.statement: A clear algorithm identifies ordered steps that satisfy a problem's requirements.
073.explanation: The design should specify how inputs are processed into the required result.

074.statement: A boundary test should use only values far away from the permitted limits.
074.explanation: Useful boundary tests include values at and just outside limits.
074.correction: Useful boundary tests include values at and just outside limits.

075.statement: An O(log n) algorithm typically grows more slowly than an O(n) algorithm as n increases.
075.explanation: A logarithmic algorithm scales more slowly than a linear one.

076.statement: An O(n²) algorithm grows more slowly than an O(n) algorithm for sufficiently large n.
076.explanation: Quadratic work grows faster than linear work as input size increases.
076.correction: Quadratic work grows faster than linear work as input size increases.

077.statement: Algorithm choice may depend on both time complexity and available memory.
077.explanation: Space use, preconditions and input characteristics all matter.

078.statement: Linear search requires all input values to be sorted.
078.explanation: It checks elements in turn and also works on unsorted data.
078.correction: It checks elements in turn and also works on unsorted data.

079.statement: Binary search can discard half of a sorted search interval after each comparison.
079.explanation: The direction of the comparison identifies the half to retain.

080.statement: In ascending bubble sort, a swap is needed whenever the left value is smaller.
080.explanation: Adjacent elements swap when the left value is greater than the right.
080.correction: Adjacent elements swap when the left value is greater than the right.

081.statement: Insertion sort grows a sorted prefix by inserting the next item into its position.
081.explanation: Earlier larger elements may be shifted to make space.

082.statement: Merge sort combines two ordered lists by always taking their larger next element.
082.explanation: Ascending merge chooses the smaller available next element.
082.correction: Ascending merge chooses the smaller available next element.

083.statement: A quicksort partition puts elements on appropriate sides of a chosen pivot.
083.explanation: Partitioning prepares the smaller subproblems for recursive sorting.

084.statement: Dijkstra's algorithm guarantees correct shortest paths with arbitrary negative edge weights.
084.explanation: Standard Dijkstra assumes non-negative edge weights.
084.correction: Standard Dijkstra assumes non-negative edge weights.

085.statement: In A* search, the score f is calculated from g plus h.
085.explanation: g is the cost so far and h estimates the remaining cost.

086.statement: A sorting algorithm and a shortest-path algorithm solve exactly the same problem.
086.explanation: Sorting orders items; pathfinding seeks routes or costs through a graph.
086.correction: Sorting orders items; pathfinding seeks routes or costs through a graph.

087.statement: Tracing an unfamiliar algorithm can reveal the first step where its state becomes incorrect.
087.explanation: Following variable changes helps pinpoint logic errors.

088.statement: A well-designed algorithm needs no tests if the pseudocode looks correct.
088.explanation: Normal, boundary and invalid cases should still be tested.
088.correction: Normal, boundary and invalid cases should still be tested.

089.statement: Assessment feedback can identify a misconception that needs correcting before the next topic.
089.explanation: Feedback and a corrected method make the assessment useful for learning.

090.statement: The CPU control unit performs arithmetic calculations instead of the ALU.
090.explanation: The ALU handles arithmetic and logic; the control unit coordinates operations.
090.correction: The ALU handles arithmetic and logic; the control unit coordinates operations.

091.statement: The Program Counter stores the address of the next instruction to fetch.

092.statement: The data bus carries memory addresses while the address bus carries values.
092.explanation: The address bus carries addresses and the data bus carries data.
092.correction: The address bus carries addresses and the data bus carries data.

093.statement: Harvard architecture has separate instruction and data memory paths.
093.explanation: This contrasts with the shared-memory organisation of von Neumann architecture.

094.statement: Doubling a processor's clock speed guarantees twice the performance on every task.
094.explanation: Core count, cache, instruction mix and other factors also affect performance.
094.correction: Core count, cache, instruction mix and other factors also affect performance.

095.statement: CPU pipelining overlaps stages of instructions to improve throughput.
095.explanation: Hazards can still cause stalls or pipeline disruption.

096.statement: Little Man Computer uses the accumulator only to store memory addresses.
096.explanation: The accumulator holds values used in arithmetic and data operations.
096.correction: The accumulator holds values used in arithmetic and data operations.

097.statement: An LMC branch instruction can change which instruction executes next.
097.explanation: Branching changes the normal sequential flow.

098.statement: An LMC loop must execute its body exactly once.
098.explanation: A branch condition can make a loop execute repeatedly or not at all.
098.correction: A branch condition can make a loop execute repeatedly or not at all.

099.statement: CISC and RISC differ in how their instruction sets are designed.
099.explanation: CISC tends towards richer instructions; RISC towards simpler regular operations.
